name: Streambed

status.note: No tagged release yet: the changelog lists 0.1.0 as upcoming, and almost all commits come from one developer since April 2026.

summary: A small Go program that copies Postgres changes into Iceberg or DuckLake tables on S3 through logical replication, and answers SQL over them through a Postgres-compatible server built on DuckDB.
intro: Streambed connects to Postgres as a logical replication subscriber, so the source needs `wal_level = logical` and nothing else. One loop reads the WAL through the `pgoutput` plugin, decodes inserts, updates and deletes, and buffers rows per table in memory. Every 10,000 rows or 2 seconds by default it writes the buffer as a Parquet file to S3 (or MinIO or another S3-compatible store) and commits a new table snapshot. Updates and deletes are copy-on-write by default: Streambed reads the affected Parquet data, drops the old rows and writes the merged result; Iceberg v2 equality deletes are an opt-in alternative. It only acknowledges a WAL position to Postgres once the rows before it are on S3, so Postgres keeps any WAL it hasn’t flushed, and `resync` backfills a table with `COPY` under a consistent snapshot.

Tables can be written as Apache Iceberg, readable by any Iceberg engine, or as DuckLake, whose catalog lives in a DuckDB or SQLite file. The built-in query server embeds DuckDB and speaks the Postgres wire protocol, so you can point `psql` at port 5433 and run analytical queries, including time travel to a past commit with `AT (TIMESTAMP => …)`. Other commands list snapshots, expire old Iceberg snapshots and compact small files. With Postgres 16 or newer it can read changes from a hot-standby replica, using the primary only to create the publication.
strengths: Very little to run: one Go binary, a Postgres with logical replication, and a bucket; no Kafka, Spark or warehouse in between
Data lands in open formats in your own bucket, as Parquet with Iceberg or DuckLake metadata, so other engines can read the same tables
Analysts query with the Postgres tools they know, through a DuckDB-backed server that answers columnar queries much faster than the row-store source
Can stream from a read replica to keep load off the primary, and keeps a snapshot per commit for time travel
limits: Very young: started in April 2026, no tagged release, and essentially one maintainer

Copy-on-write rewrites Parquet data for every batch of updates and deletes, and frequent small commits pile up Iceberg metadata and small files; the author’s own benchmark found DuckLake about 38 times faster than Iceberg on an update-heavy load (7 s against 269 s)
Time-travel timestamps are Streambed’s commit times, not the original Postgres transaction times, and expired snapshots can’t be queried
Equality-delete (merge-on-read) mode is one-way: once a table has equality deletes, Streambed refuses to start in copy-on-write mode

snippet.title: Stream a local Postgres into Iceberg on MinIO and query it with psql
source: # analytical queries go to DuckDB over Parquet, not to your primary

story: Analytical queries on a production Postgres database eventually become too slow to run there but too important to drop. The usual answer is an ETL pipeline into a warehouse, with Spark, Airflow or a managed connector service, hours of delay and a copy that can drift from the source. Vignesh (viggy28 on GitHub), formerly at Cloudflare and a co-founder of Omnigres, started Streambed in April 2026 to skip that pipeline: subscribe to the WAL directly and write open table files to S3, seconds behind production.

The first version wrote only Iceberg. In August 2026 he added DuckLake as a second target after finding that change-data capture, with its stream of small commits, multiplies Iceberg metadata files and small Parquet files; DuckLake keeps that metadata in a database instead and fit the write path, which already used DuckDB. Reading from a hot-standby replica followed in September.

choices.choice: Logical replication straight into table files
choices.why: Skipping Kafka, batch jobs and Spark removes the moving parts and the hours of delay of a classic pipeline, and keeps the data seconds behind the source.

choices.choice: A Postgres wire protocol query server on DuckDB
choices.why: Users keep `psql` and their Postgres tools, while DuckDB’s columnar engine on Parquet handles the analytical queries that are slow on Postgres’s row storage.

choices.choice: One goroutine for the whole pipeline
choices.why: Reading, decoding, buffering, flushing and acknowledging in one loop, with no channels between stages, keeps ordering and backpressure easy to reason about.
Small, frequent CDC commits create a lot of Iceberg metadata in object storage; a catalog in a database gives a shorter commit path, while Iceberg remains for engine interoperability.
